formNote: Attach 잖아요 straight onto a plain verb or adjective stem; for past tense use 았/었잖아요. It reminds the listener of something you both already know, so it can sound a bit blaming if overused. There is no truly formal 합니다-style version, so reserve it for casual and 요 speech.
usage: That place is expensive, you know.
Fridays are always packed, you know.
examples: 야, 그 사람 너 좋아하잖아. 왜 모른 척해?
Dude, he likes you, you know. Why act clueless?
dating gossip
오늘 팀장님 기분 안 좋잖아요. 보고는 내일 하죠.
The team lead's in a bad mood today, you know. Let's report tomorrow.
office read-the-room
배달비 또 올랐잖아. 그냥 가서 먹자.
Delivery fees went up again, you know. Let's just eat there.
money talk
mistakes: Do not use 잖아요 for brand-new info the listener has never heard; it implies they should already know.
It can sound naggy with elders or strangers, so keep it for friends and close coworkers.

formNote: Add 거든요 to a plain verb or adjective stem to give a reason or background the listener doesn't know yet; for past use 았/었거든요. It often answers a 왜? or sets up a story, and the 요 keeps it polite. Said flatly to a stranger it can sound slightly defensive, so mind your tone.
usage: 저 오늘 못 가요. 약속이 있거든요.
I can't come today. I have plans, see.
그 카페 자주 가. 분위기가 좋거든.
I go to that cafe a lot. The vibe's great, see.
I didn't sleep last night, see.
Actually I'm vegetarian, just so you know.
examples: 왜 이렇게 피곤해 보이냐고요? 어제 밤새 일했거든요.
Why do I look so tired? Because I pulled an all-nighter at work.
office context
저 이번 달은 좀 아껴야 돼요. 월세 올랐거든요.
I have to save this month. My rent went up, see.
money/rent
그 사람한테 연락 안 해. 나 차였거든.
I'm not texting him. I got dumped, see.
dating
mistakes: 거든요 introduces info the listener does NOT yet know, unlike 잖아요 which assumes they do.
Avoid a sharp falling tone with strangers; it can come off as defensive or curt.

formNote: Attach 더라고요 to a plain verb or adjective stem to report something you personally saw, felt, or realized in the past. Because it is your own discovery, you normally do not use it about your own feelings or actions you were already aware of. The 고 is often dropped in speech, giving the very casual 더라.
usage: When I went, it was better than I thought.
The wait at that restaurant was really long.
The new hire is good at the job, I noticed.
Living alone turned out to be lonely.
examples: 어제 소개팅 했는데 의외로 대화가 잘 통하더라고요.
I had a blind date yesterday, and we surprisingly clicked.
dating
그 동네 가 봤는데 월세가 생각보다 싸더라고요.
I checked out that neighborhood; rent was cheaper than expected.
rent hunting
회식 가 보니까 분위기가 생각보다 편하더라고요.
The company dinner turned out more relaxed than I expected.
drinking culture
mistakes: Do not use 더라고요 for your own ongoing emotions you already knew about; it's for fresh discovery.
It must be something you experienced yourself, not secondhand news you only heard about.

formNote: Add ㄹ래요 after a vowel stem and 을래요 after a consonant stem; ㄹ-final stems keep their ㄹ and just add 래요 with no 으 (놀다 to 놀래요). As a question it casually suggests doing something together or asks the listener's will. As a statement it states your own intention (저 갈래요 = I'll go / I wanna go).
examples: 주말에 시간 되면 영화 볼래?
If you're free this weekend, wanna catch a movie?
asking someone out
점심 같이 시켜 먹을래요?
Wanna order delivery for lunch together?
office/delivery
오늘 한 잔 할래? 1차만 가볍게.
Wanna grab a drink today? Just one round, light.
drinking culture
mistakes: Do not use ㄹ래요? to invite someone clearly above you; use 같이 가시겠어요? or 같이 가실래요? to soften it.
ㄹ-final stems take just 래요 with no 으, so 놀다 becomes 놀래요, never 놀을래요.

formNote: Verbs take 는데요; adjectives take ㄴ데요 after a vowel and 은데요 after a consonant (좋다 to 좋은데요). 있다/없다 and past tense use 는데요 (재밌었는데요). Ending a sentence on 는데요 softens it, hints at a 'but...', or invites the other person to respond.
usage: I'm kind of busy right now, though.
I don't really know about that, though.
examples: 그 사람 나쁘진 않은데요, 좀 제 스타일은 아니에요.
He's not bad, but he's just not my type.
dating, soft no
디자인은 괜찮은데요, 마감일은 좀 무리일 것 같아요.
The design's fine, but the deadline seems tight.
office pushback
저 지금 카페에 있는데, 너 어디야?
I'm at the cafe right now, where are you?
casual, leading on
mistakes: Don't put 는 on adjectives: it's 바쁜데요, not 바쁘는데요.
It rarely stands alone with strangers without context; the trailing tone implies more is coming.

english: I'm planning to / I intend to
formNote: Add 려고요 after a vowel stem and 으려고요 after a consonant stem to state your own intention, often as a reply to 'what are you going to do?'. It's the shortened, conversational form of 려고 해요. Use it only about your own plans, not someone else's.
usage: I'm just gonna rest at home today.
I'm trying to save up some money.
I'm planning to switch jobs next year.
examples: 이번 주말엔 소개팅 한번 나가 보려고요.
I'm thinking of trying a blind date this weekend.
dating plan
월세 너무 비싸서 좀 더 싼 데로 이사 가려고요.
Rent's too high, so I'm planning to move somewhere cheaper.
rent
오늘 회식은 1차만 가고 빠지려고요.
I'm planning to leave after the first round of the work dinner.
drinking culture
mistakes: Use it only for your own intentions; for someone else's plan use 려나 봐요 or just ask them.
Don't confuse it with 으러: 사러 가요 = go in order to buy, but 사려고요 = I'm planning to buy.

formNote: Attach 는 중이에요 to a plain verb stem to say an action is in progress right now; ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ (만들다 to 만드는 중이에요). With a noun, use N 중이에요 (회의 중이에요 = in a meeting). It is not used with adjectives or with states like 알다.
usage: I'm on my way right now.
I'm in the middle of eating.
I'm in the middle of working.
examples: 미안, 지금 일하는 중이라 이따 톡할게.
Sorry, I'm working right now, I'll text you later.
messaging
거의 다 왔어요, 지금 엘리베이터 타는 중이에요.
I'm almost there, getting in the elevator now.
running late
다이어트 중이라 오늘은 치킨 패스할게.
I'm on a diet, so I'll pass on the chicken today.
social/food
mistakes: Don't use it with adjectives or stative verbs; 아는 중이에요 is wrong.
For a relaxed near-future state, 가는 중 means literally en route, not 'about to leave'.

formNote: Verbs and 있다/없다 take 나 봐요 (오나 봐요). Descriptive adjectives usually take ㄴ가/은가 봐요 (바쁜가 봐요, 좋은가 봐요), and nouns take 인가 봐요. It expresses a guess based on something you observed, so don't use it about your own clear feelings.
usage: Seems like those two are dating.
examples: 걔가 읽씹하네. 나한테 관심 없나 봐.
He left my message on read. Guess he's not into me.
dating
팀장님 아직 안 가셨네요. 마감 때문에 바쁜가 봐요.
The team lead hasn't left yet. Must be busy with the deadline.
office
다들 그 집 올리던데, 거기 핫플인가 봐요.
Everyone's posting that place; must be the new hotspot.
social media
mistakes: Use ㄴ가/은가 봐요 (not 나 봐요) for plain adjectives: 좋은가 봐요, not 좋나 봐요.
Don't use it about your own feelings you already know; 나 슬픈가 봐 sounds odd as a direct statement.

formNote: Add ㄹ 뻔했어요 after a vowel stem and 을 뻔했어요 after a consonant stem; ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ. It describes something that nearly happened but did NOT, almost always a near-miss or close call. It is fixed in the past tense (했어요).
examples: 지하철 놓칠 뻔했는데 겨우 탔어요.
I almost missed the subway but barely made it.
commute
술 마시고 전 남친한테 연락할 뻔했잖아.
I almost texted my ex while drunk, you know.
drinking/dating
마감 깜빡할 뻔했는데 알림 덕분에 살았어요.
I almost forgot the deadline; the reminder saved me.
office
mistakes: It means the thing did NOT happen; if it actually happened, don't use 뻔했어요.
Keep it in the past: it's 늦을 뻔했어요, never 늦을 뻔해요.

formNote: Verbs take 는 척하다 (자는 척해요); adjectives take ㄴ/은 척하다 (예쁜 척해요, 괜찮은 척해요); past actions take 은/ㄴ 척하다 (안 들은 척해요). It means putting on an act you don't really feel or do. 척 can be swapped for the slightly more casual 체.
usage: I pretended I didn't hear it.
examples: 전 남친 마주쳤는데 그냥 못 본 척하고 지나갔어.
I ran into my ex and just walked past pretending not to see him.
dating
회식에서 안 취한 척했는데 사실 엄청 취했어요.
I acted sober at the work dinner but I was actually wasted.
drinking culture
부장님 농담에 다들 재밌는 척 웃었어요.
Everyone laughed like the boss's joke was funny.
office politics
mistakes: Match the modifier to the word type: 자는 척 (verb) but 예쁜 척 (adjective), not 예쁘는 척.
It implies the act is fake, so don't use it when the thing is genuinely true.
